START HERE
Your route from beginner to prepared
trader
This is a practical course for Adrian: a Canadian beginner learning US-stock day trading with
TradingView. Start with simulated money. The objective is to learn an execution process,
measure whether it has an edge after costs, and decide whether live trading is appropriate.
Profit is a possible outcome, not a course promise.

HOW TO FOLLOW ALONG
Read one lesson, complete its exercise, and check your answer before moving on.
Keep a notebook or use the printable worksheets. A lesson is finished when you can
demonstrate the task, not when you have skimmed the page.
Platform and policy references were checked September 29, 2026. Buttons, plan access, fees and account rules can

pages.title: What success looks like
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
03  /  37
COURSE MAP
What success looks like
Five skills you should leave with
• Find the correct stock, exchange, session and data source before looking for a signal.
• Explain exactly what confirms an entry and what invalidates it.
• Calculate share quantity from risk and available cash, then enter the correct order.
• Manage exits without increasing the loss budget or confusing an order with a fill.
• Keep honest records and stop when the evidence does not support your strategy.
A realistic definition of making money
A single profitable trade can happen by chance. A useful trading process must survive losses,
realistic transaction costs and different market conditions. Your early goal is to lose as little
simulated money as necessary while learning. Do not use trading profits to plan rent, debt
payments or a fixed daily wage.
Milestone
Evidence
Platform competence
Correctly complete at least ten simulated order drills.
Rule competence
Recognize qualified setups and no-trade cases without looking ahead.
Process competence
Maintain a journal and follow the same rules for 30-50 forward-paper trades.
Readiness review
Evaluate costs, drawdown, discipline and uncertainty; passing does not prove
future profitability.
YOUR COURSE CONTRACT
I will not risk money I need for living expenses. I will not borrow to complete this
course. I will use one testable setup, log every attempt and stop when my rules say
stop.
Write your reason for learning, the hours you can practise, and the maximum amount you could afford to lose if you
eventually decide to trade live. Leave the live amount blank if you cannot yet answer it honestly.

pages.title: What a day trade actually is
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
04  /  37
01 / FOUNDATIONS
What a day trade actually is
A day trade opens and closes a position within the same trading day. A long trade buys
shares first and later sells them. You profit if your average exit price is higher than your
average entry price by enough to cover all costs. A falling stock is not automatically a
bargain, and an exciting headline does not guarantee a price rise.
Keep the first version simple
This course uses liquid US-listed stocks or unlevered broad-market ETFs, whole-share long
positions, and regular market hours. Short selling, options, leveraged ETFs, futures and
crypto need additional knowledge and different risk controls. A chart that looks similar can
represent a very different product.
Role
What it does
TradingView
Displays charts, drawing tools, alerts and supported trading connections.
Broker
Holds the account and receives, routes or simulates orders.
Data provider
Supplies prices, quotes and volume; coverage and delay matter.
Your strategy
Defines an observable entry, invalidation, risk and exit.
You / ADRIAN
Researches and checks a plan. Approval and broker results remain separate.
When to practise
The NYSE core equity session is normally 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM Eastern Time on US trading
days, with exchange holidays and occasional early closes. Toronto is in the same Eastern
time zone. Verify the calendar each day. Premarket and after-hours trading have different
liquidity and order restrictions. [S1]
CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
If you buy 20 shares at $50 and sell all 20 at $50.50, gross profit is $10. If total costs
are $3, net profit is $7. Buying and selling does not itself guarantee that you made
money.

pages.title: The prices behind the chart
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
05  /  37
01 / FOUNDATIONS
The prices behind the chart
Bid, ask and spread
The bid is a displayed price someone is willing to pay. The ask is a displayed price someone
is willing to accept. The spread is ask minus bid. A chart often shows the last traded price; it
does not promise you can buy or sell at that price. A marketable buy generally trades against
available asks and a marketable sell against available bids.
Fictional quote
Meaning
Bid $50.00 / ask $50.04
Spread = $0.04 per share.
Buy 100 at $50.04, immediately sell at
$50.00
Approximately $4 lost to spread before other costs.
Chart last trade $50.02
Not necessarily an executable price for your order.
Only ten shares available at the displayed
ask
A larger order may fill at multiple prices.
Costs that quietly erase an edge
Commissions, spread, slippage, exchange or regulatory charges, data subscriptions and
CAD/USD conversion can all matter. Slippage is the difference between an expected and
actual fill. A fixed monthly service cost should be counted in your overall results, even if it is
not assigned to every trade.
Liquidity, gaps and halts
Liquid markets usually have more active participants and more available trading interest.
Liquidity can vanish around news. A stock can jump across your stop price or halt trading. A
stop is an exit instruction, not insurance that a loss cannot exceed the planned amount. [S2]
DO THIS NOW
Look at one paper quote and calculate its spread. Then compare that spread with your
intended stop distance. A $0.10 spread is already 20% of a $0.50 stop distance.
Record the ratio; skip if trading friction makes the setup impractical.

pages.title: Set up the right account and records
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
06  /  37
01 / CANADA
Set up the right account and records
Paper accounts are your starting point
Your Alpaca Paper Only account is for simulated trades. Alpaca documents that paper-only
access is globally available and uses IEX data. Its current brokerage eligibility guidance
excludes Canadian residents from live accounts. Do not assume paper eligibility also grants
live brokerage access. [S3, S4]
Before considering live trading
Choose a broker that accepts your residence and supports the products, order types and
data you need. Ask which legal entity carries the account, whether it is cash or margin, what
settlement and day-trading restrictions apply, and whether your intended API workflow is
permitted. Do not copy a US social-media account rule into a Canadian account without
confirmation.
Interactive Brokers Canada offers trading APIs, but documents restrictions on Canadian
residents using APIs for products traded on Canadian exchanges or marketplaces. That is
relevant to automation; it does not mean every manual Canadian-stock trade is prohibited.
Confirm your exact use case with the broker. [S5]
Taxes and settlement
Canadian cash-stock settlement generally moved to T+1: the business day after the trade,
subject to the instrument and holidays. Selling does not necessarily make funds immediately
reusable under every cash-account rule. Ask your broker. [S6]
Trading income may be business income or capital gains depending on the facts. Do not
assume frequent trading in a TFSA is automatically tax-free: CRA says a TFSA trust carrying
on a business can be taxable on business income and related gains. Keep records and
consult a Canadian tax professional before trading actively in a registered account. [S7]
KEEP THESE RECORDS
Date, symbol, quantity, entry and exit fills, fees, CAD/USD conversions, account
statements and your trading journal. Use one consistent reporting currency for
performance calculations; currency changes can affect your actual CAD result.

pages.title: Build a clean TradingView workspace
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
07  /  37
02 / TRADINGVIEW
Build a clean TradingView workspace
Open TradingView in a browser, sign in, and open Supercharts. The following is a
follow-along workflow; menu positions can differ by device and account version. Do not buy a
subscription until you know which features you actually need.
• Search for a symbol. Check its full company name, exchange and currency so you do not
analyse an unrelated instrument with a similar ticker.
• Choose standard candlesticks. Keep the background and candle colours easy to read.
• Set the chart time zone to America/Toronto or its equivalent Eastern-time choice.
• Use a daily chart to identify broad levels, then a 15-minute chart for structure and a
5-minute chart for the course setup.
• Choose regular-session data for this course. If you later add extended hours, label the
change in your rules and journal.
• Add Volume. Optionally add a session-anchored VWAP. Avoid filling the chart with many
indicators.
• Save a named layout and create a short watchlist of liquid instruments you can follow
consistently.
Verify the data before trusting a signal
Look for delayed-data notices, the feed/exchange label and the timestamp of the latest bar.
A subscription to charts is not always an entitlement to every exchange feed. Quotes in
TradingView, your broker and ADRIAN can differ because their sources or sessions differ.
WORKSPACE PASS TEST
You can point to the symbol, exchange, time zone, session, timeframe, current data
status and saved layout. If one of those is unknown, setup is not finished.
TradingView documents Supercharts access, Trade and Replay controls in its demo-features guide. Plan access can
vary. [S8]

pages.title: Connect the simulator and set realistic limits
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
08  /  37
02 / PAPER PRACTICE
Connect the simulator and set realistic
limits
Use TradingView Paper Trading for manual order practice. Open the Trade area or Trading
Panel, select Paper Trading and connect. Check that the active account explicitly says Paper
Trading before submitting anything. The simulator tracks orders and positions; money is
virtual. [S9]
A small-account practice configuration
Use a paper balance close to what you could realistically afford eventually, such as USD
$2,000. If your existing Alpaca paper balance is $100,000, you can still restrict yourself to a
$2,000 practice budget. A large simulated balance must not teach you to take unaffordable
positions.
Course training rule
Starting value
Leverage
None; position cost must fit practice cash.
Risk per trade
0.25% of practice equity.
Daily loss stop
1% of practice equity, including costs.
Attempts per day
Maximum three; fewer if the loss stop is reached.
Concurrent positions
One.
Trading window
First practise 9:45-11:00 AM Toronto; be flat before
regular-session close.
These are conservative teaching defaults, not a universal optimal strategy. TradingView
paper leverage may be preconfigured; check it rather than assuming 1:1. Commission
settings can simulate trading charges. Use your intended broker fee schedule where
available and separately log spread/slippage. [S10, S11]
IMPORTANT ACCOUNT DISTINCTION
TradingView Paper Trading and Alpaca Paper Trading are separate simulators. They
do not automatically share cash, positions or journals. Choose one execution account
per practice session and label every trade with the account used.

pages.title: Practise without seeing the future
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
09  /  37
02 / REPLAY
Practise without seeing the future
Two different practice modes
Forward paper trading follows the market as new data arrives. Replay practice advances
historical bars so you can make decisions without knowing what happens next. Both teach
useful skills, but neither reproduces every live execution constraint.
• Open Bar Replay from the chart controls and select a past session you have not already
studied.
• Move to a point before the opening-range setup is complete. Advance one bar at a time.
• Write your entry, stop, target and quantity before revealing the next bar.
• Use the dedicated Replay Trading mode if available to your account. TradingView
documents it as separate from Paper Trading.
• Do not send an ordinary paper or connected-broker order just because the displayed chart
is in the past: standard trading-panel orders and alerts can still use real-time data.
• Save your journal and screenshots before leaving the replay session; replay-trade results
may only be available in that session. [S12, S13]
Prevent the most common replay mistake
Do not choose only days that have obvious trends, skip your losing signals, or move your
entry backward after seeing a rally. Include quiet days, failed breakouts and sessions with no
qualifying trade. If you change a rule, give it a new strategy version and test it on later
unseen sessions.
EXERCISE
Replay three different days. On each, record one qualified setup or one clear reason
for no trade. Do not count a hypothetical fill merely because a candle touched your
limit; historical bar data can leave execution order and liquidity ambiguous.

pages.title: Candles tell a small story, not the future
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
10  /  37
03 / CHART READING
Candles tell a small story, not the future
HIGH
LOW
OPEN
CLOSE
HIGH
LOW
OPEN
CLOSE
UP CANDLE
DOWN CANDLE
Each candle summarises open, high, low and close for its timeframe. Its body connects open
and close; its wicks show the remaining range. An up candle closes above its open; a down
candle closes below. Colours are configurable. A 5-minute candle still forming can look
convincing and finish very differently.
Read the sequence
Ask whether recent swings are making higher highs and higher lows, lower highs and lower
lows, or moving inside a range. A single long wick is not an automatic reversal. Put it beside
nearby levels, liquidity and the broader session.
Do not confuse a candle with a quote
OHLC data describes transactions over a period. It does not show the exact current bid/ask,
all available size, or the order in which both a stop and target were touched inside the same
bar. Use actual order and fill records for execution results.
CHECK
A candle opens at $50.00, reaches $50.40, falls to $49.80 and closes at $50.10. Is it
an up candle? Yes. Did it prove buyers controlled the whole period? No; price moved
in both directions.

pages.title: Support, resistance and market context
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
11  /  37
03 / LEVELS
Support, resistance and market context
Support is an area where buying has previously interrupted a decline. Resistance is an area
where selling has previously interrupted a rise. They are zones of observed behaviour, not
invisible walls. Price can pass through either.
Draw fewer, better levels
• On the daily chart, mark the previous session high and low and the closest obvious swing
level.
• On the intraday chart, mark the first 15-minute opening-range high and low once that
range is complete.
• Use horizontal lines and label their origin. Avoid drawing a line through every minor wiggle.
• Identify the next resistance above a potential long entry. A nearby obstacle can leave too
little reward for the risk.
Trend, range or confusion?
A trend has directional structure. A range has repeated movement between areas. Choppy
action flips direction and makes several apparent breakouts fail. The same entry rule may
behave differently in each. The course setup is a research hypothesis, not a reason to force
trades in every condition.
Observation
Response
Clear levels and room above entry
Continue checking the setup.
Price repeatedly crosses the same level
Expect false signals; skipping is reasonable.
Target is beyond nearby resistance
Recalculate realistic reward or skip.
Important level differs across feeds
Confirm session and source before acting.
EXERCISE
Mark only three important levels on a chart. Explain in one sentence why each
matters. If you cannot explain a line, remove it. Record the chart timeframe and
session so you can reproduce the markings.

pages.title: Use indicators as context
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
12  /  37
03 / VOLUME & VWAP
Use indicators as context
Volume is participation, not a forecast
Volume counts shares traded in the feed for the period. Larger volume can make a price
move more interesting, but it does not tell you who will win the next trade. Compare like with
like: a 5-minute bar with completed 5-minute bars, not with an entire day.
Intraday volume has a time-of-day pattern. A bar near the open often has more volume than
a midday bar. A simple comparison to the immediately preceding bars is a basic training
rule, not a fully adjusted measure of relative volume. Keep the definition unchanged during
your initial test.
Session VWAP
VWAP is a volume-weighted price average. With a Session anchor, its calculation resets with
the configured session. It can help describe whether price is trading above or below the
session average; it lags and is not a buy button. Check the anchor and session settings
rather than treating every line called VWAP as equivalent. [S14]
Your Alpaca feed
Alpaca Paper Only users are entitled to IEX data. IEX is one venue, not consolidated
full-market trading volume. A chart using another feed can show different volume or levels.
Analyse your strategy using a consistent feed and do not combine one venue’s volume with a
whole-market threshold without testing that choice. [S3]
EXERCISE
Record the feed name, timeframe, current-bar volume, comparison-bar average and
resulting ratio. Example: 150,000 / 100,000 = 1.5 times. This ratio describes observed
participation; it is not a 75% probability of profit.

pages.title: Know what your order can and cannot do
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
13  /  37
04 / ORDER SKILLS
Know what your order can and cannot
do
Order
What it asks for
Main limitation
Market
Trade at available prices now.
Execution price can differ from the chart.
Limit buy
Buy at the limit or lower.
May not fill, even if you want the position.
Buy stop
Activate after a specified trigger.
Once marketable, price can run beyond the
trigger.
Stop-loss sell
Activate an exit if the stop triggers.
A stop-market exit has no guaranteed fill
price.
Stop-limit sell
After trigger, sell only at the limit or better.
Can remain unfilled during a sharp fall.
Brackets and linked exits
A bracket combines an entry with protective stop and target instructions. Exact activation,
partial-fill behaviour and cancellation links depend on the broker. Verify which exit orders are
actually working after your entry fills. Do not assume that drawing a stop on a chart created
an order. Investor.gov explains why stops and stop-limits have different execution risks. [S2]
Order status vocabulary
Submitted or accepted means the broker received the instruction. Open means it remains
working. Partially filled means only some quantity executed. Filled means the reported
quantity executed. Cancel requested is not the same as canceled. Rejected means the
broker did not accept that order.
ORDER DRILL
In paper trading, practise a small limit entry, an unfilled order cancellation, a
protective stop, and a linked target. Read the actual order rows after every action.
Before trying again after a connection error, check whether the first order already
exists.

pages.title: Size from the stop, not from excitement
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
14  /  37
04 / RISK MATH
Size from the stop, not from excitement
The basic long-position calculation
Dollar risk budget = practice equity × risk percentage. Stop distance = planned entry minus
planned stop. Whole shares = round down(dollar risk budget / stop distance). Also cap shares
at what available practice cash can buy. Use the maximum allowed entry price when a limit
could fill above your reference.
Worked example
Calculation
Practice equity
USD $2,000
Risk percentage
0.25% = 0.0025
Risk budget
$2,000 × 0.0025 = $5
Entry / stop
$50.40 / $49.90
Stop distance
$0.50 per share
Quantity before cost reserve
floor($5 / $0.50) = 10 shares
Cash needed
10 × $50.40 = $504
Planned gross stop loss
10 × $0.50 = $5
Costs consume part of your loss budget. If you reserve $1 for all-in trading friction, only $4
remains for price risk: floor($4 / $0.50) = 8 shares. That gives $4 planned price loss plus a $1
reserve. Real slippage or gaps can still produce a larger loss.
DO NOT REVERSE THE PROCESS
Choose a stop that reflects invalidation, then calculate size. Do not place an artificially
tight stop just to buy more shares. If the required position does not fit your cash or
risk limits, skip.
If you approve ADRIAN’s proposal, use the quantity and maximum price stated in that proposal. Your manual course
budget can be smaller than ADRIAN’s configured account-equity budget; align them in Settings before comparing
results.

pages.title: R, reward and the daily stop
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
15  /  37
04 / RISK LIMITS
R, reward and the daily stop
R is one unit of planned price risk. If the plan risks $5 before costs, +$10 gross is +2R and
-$5 gross is -1R. Costs lower realised net R. A trade with a 2R target is not automatically
profitable: it might lose too often or fail to reach its target.
Plan
Result
Entry $50.40; stop $49.90
Risk per share $0.50.
Target $51.40
Potential reward $1.00; gross reward/risk = 2.
Next resistance $50.70
Only $0.30 room; gross reward/risk = 0.6.
Daily loss limit on $2,000 at 1%
$20. Stop trading if realised losses plus costs reach it.
Add a gate before every entry
Check that the next trade’s worst planned loss plus cost reserve fits inside the remaining
daily loss budget. If $17 has already been lost and the cap is $20, a new $5-risk trade does
not fit. This remains true even if you feel certain about the next setup.
Drawdown is your loss from a prior peak
If equity rises to $2,100 and later drops to $1,995, drawdown from that peak is $105, or 5%.
Recovering a 10% loss requires an 11.1% gain on the reduced capital. Larger losses become
progressively harder to recover.
EXERCISE
With a $3,000 practice account, 0.25% risk, an entry at $25.20 and stop at $24.90,
calculate quantity before costs. Answer: risk budget $7.50, distance $0.30, quantity
25 shares, cash $630. Reserve costs before using that full size.

pages.title: Opening-range breakout: the research rules
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
16  /  37
05 / ONE TESTABLE SETUP
Opening-range breakout: the research
rules
We will test one long-only opening-range breakout. This is a teaching strategy to study, not a
validated money-making system. Its rules must remain unchanged for the first test batch so
that you can tell whether the results mean anything.
Rule
Course test version 1.0
Universe
A small, preselected watchlist of liquid US stocks or unlevered ETFs; no penny stocks.
Opening range
High and low of regular-session bars from 9:30 through 9:44:59 Toronto. Complete it
before acting.
Signal window
9:45-11:00 AM; 5-minute standard candles.
Confirmation
A completed 5-minute candle closes above the range high and session VWAP. Its volume
exceeds the mean of the preceding three completed 5-minute bars.
Entry
After that close, use a paper limit order with a predefined maximum price. Skip if price
exceeds it; cancel an unfilled entry after one 5-minute bar.
Stop
Below a predefined structural low or the range boundary; write the exact invalidation
before entry.
Target
At least 2 times stop distance above entry, with enough room before obvious resistance.
End of session
Exit remaining exposure and cancel entry orders before regular-session close. The course
does not hold overnight.
The first signal cannot be placed before its confirmation bar closes. Your fill may occur on the next bar or not occur at
all. VWAP and volume filters are hypotheses; they must earn their place through testing. Use regular-session data
consistently.

pages.title: See the setup before you trade it
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
17  /  37
05 / THE VISUAL PLAN
See the setup before you trade it
49.50
50.00
50.50
51.00
51.50
OR HIGH / 50.40
STOP / 49.90
TARGET / 51.40
9:30
10:00
10:30
11:00
FICTIONAL PRICE PATH - TEACHING DIAGRAM
This fictional chart illustrates a possible path, not a prediction. The opening-range high is
$50.40. A completed confirmation candle breaks above the level; price then pulls back and
moves higher. The drawn stop is $49.90 and illustrative target is $51.40.
What would make this tradable in the course?
• The opening range is complete and the signal candle meets the fixed VWAP and volume
rules.
• The quote is fresh, spread is practical, and the stock is not halted.
• The permitted entry price, structural stop and realistic target still offer the planned
reward/risk.
• Quantity fits your cash, per-trade risk and remaining daily loss budget.
• You can watch the trade and verify that the actual stop/target orders exist after entry.
WHAT THE DIAGRAM CANNOT SHOW
This picture omits actual quotes, available size, news, VWAP and volume. A
nice-looking price path alone is insufficient evidence to trade. If those checks are
missing, your answer is WAIT or SKIP.
Exercise: point to the range high, the earliest possible confirmation, the invalidation area and the target. Then explain
why buying the final high candle is not the same trade as the original plan.

pages.title: A fictional winning paper trade
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
18  /  37
05 / WORKED EXAMPLE
A fictional winning paper trade
Before entry
Written plan
Account / budget
$2,000 practice equity; $5 total risk allowance.
Candidate
Fictional stock XYZ; regular session; fresh quote.
Reference / maximum entry
$50.40 / $50.40 for this example.
Stop / target
$49.90 / $51.40.
Size
8 shares after reserving $1 of the $5 risk budget for costs.
Confirmation
Completed candle above the range and VWAP; volume rule met; no
nearby target obstacle.
Execution record
At 9:50, the confirmation bar is complete. You submit the paper limit order. Eight shares fill
at $50.40. Verify that the protective exit covers eight shares and that the target is working.
Do not describe the entry as filled until the order record confirms it.
Later, all eight shares exit at the target of $51.40. Gross profit is 8 × ($51.40 - $50.40) = $8.
If total actual trading friction is $1, net profit is $7. Planned price risk was $4, so gross R is
+2 and net R is +1.75.
What made it a good practice trade?
The plan was written first, the size fit the budget, and the orders matched the plan. Those
qualities can also exist in a losing trade. Do not conclude from this one outcome that the
rules are profitable.
JOURNAL LINE
Record planned entry, actual fill, stop, target, quantity, costs, timestamps, net P/L, net
R and whether every rule was followed. Save one before-entry and one after-exit
screenshot. All amounts here are invented for instruction.

FICTIONAL PRICE PATH - TEACHING DIAGRAM
Use the same $50.40 entry, $49.90 stop and eight-share position. This time the breakout
fails. If the stop exit fills at $49.90, gross loss is $4. With $1 total costs, net loss is $5. That is
a controlled planned loss, not proof that the strategy is broken.
A stop-price gap changes the result
Suppose a sharp move means the stop-market order fills at $49.70 instead. Gross loss is 8 ×
($50.40 - $49.70) = $5.60. With $1 costs, net loss is $6.60. The stop instruction existed, but
its trigger price did not guarantee the fill price. [S2]
The action that makes the lesson worse
Moving the stop down to avoid admitting a loss increases risk beyond the approved plan.
Buying more merely because the stock is falling adds exposure. Neither action improves the
original setup’s evidence.
AFTER THE LOSS
Confirm you are flat, check for leftover orders, calculate actual costs and remaining
daily budget, and journal the result. Take a short break. A new trade needs a new
qualifying signal; recovering the loss is not an entry rule.

pages.title: Skipping is an active trading decision
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
20  /  37
05 / NO-TRADE SKILLS
Skipping is an active trading decision
Reason to skip
What to do instead
No fresh quote or feed status unknown
Fix or verify the data; do not assume the last bar is current.
Spread consumes too much of the stop distance
Choose a more practical instrument or wait.
No volume confirmation / unfinished candle
Wait for the planned confirmation; do not predict the close.
Price beyond the approved maximum
Cancel or skip. Recalculate a new plan separately.
Target blocked by nearby resistance
Reject unrealistic reward assumptions.
Scheduled earnings or major announcement
For this beginner test, skip that symbol/session rather than
improvise around news.
Daily limit hit or remaining budget too small
Stop for the day.
You cannot monitor, are angry or are tired
Do not enter. Your attention is part of the setup.
News needs a timestamp
A headline can be stale, syndicated, corrected or already reflected in price. Verify the
publication time and primary source when possible. A story title is not evidence that price
must move in a particular direction. Put scheduled economic releases and company earnings
on your preparation checklist.
EXERCISE
Find three attractive-looking charts that fail at least one rule. Write the failure clearly.
A no-trade log helps distinguish a disciplined skip from simply missing a good signal.
Do not lower the rules just because you have not traded yet.

pages.title: The first 90 minutes, step by step
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
21  /  37
06 / YOUR DAILY ROUTINE
The first 90 minutes, step by step
Toronto time
Task
9:00-9:15
Confirm calendar, account mode, feed status and connection. Review scheduled news. Start
a new journal page.
9:15-9:30
Select no more than three watch candidates. Mark daily levels. Write per-trade and daily risk
limits.
9:30-9:45
Observe. Let the opening range form. Do not treat the incomplete range as final.
9:45-11:00
Check completed 5-minute signals against the rules. Take up to three qualified attempts
within budget, or none.
After every fill
Verify quantity, working exits and remaining budget. Log actual fills, not assumptions.
11:00
Stop taking new signals for this course version. Manage any remaining position under its
written plan.
Before session
close
Be flat according to your plan, confirm no unwanted entry orders remain, and complete the
journal.
Do not turn practice into an all-day hunt
A limited window reduces fatigue and gives you more comparable observations. A trade after
your defined window belongs to another strategy version, even if it makes money. If your
schedule cannot support morning practice, choose and test a different fixed window rather
than hopping between windows.
DAILY SCORE
Give yourself one point each for: verified data, written plan, correct size, verified exits
and complete journal. A five-point losing day can be better training than a profitable
day with no controls.

pages.title: Manage the trade without rewriting it
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
22  /  37
06 / MANAGEMENT
Manage the trade without rewriting it
Once the entry fills
• Confirm actual quantity and average fill. Compare the fill with the planned risk and
maximum price.
• Confirm the protective exit covers the open position and the linked target has the expected
price and status.
• Do not widen the stop. If you reduce risk or take an early exit, document the rule that
allowed it.
• Watch order statuses and the account position, not only the chart. A canceled or rejected
exit requires immediate attention.
• Before manually closing a bracketed position, follow the broker’s documented exit/cancel
workflow to avoid leaving a sell order that could later open an unwanted position.
Partial profits are optional, not magic
For the initial course test, use one fixed target or the defined stop. Taking half at 1R and half
at 2R changes both average win and exposure. Test it as a different version instead of
deciding differently on every trade.
Time-based exit
Decide before entry whether a stalled trade has a time stop. For example, a later strategy
version could exit after three completed 5-minute bars without meaningful progress. Do not
add that rule retroactively because a trade feels uncomfortable. Always resolve remaining
exposure before the course’s end-of-session boundary.
IF THE CONNECTION FAILS
Do not blindly resubmit. Check the broker directly for positions and working orders.
Use its official support or order-management tools if needed. The broker’s actual
record determines what exists; a frozen local screen cannot establish that you are flat.

pages.title: Record decisions and fills honestly
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
23  /  37
07 / THE JOURNAL
Record decisions and fills honestly
A useful journal makes your process auditable. Without it, you will remember the large
winners, forget the small losses, and struggle to know whether a change helped. Record
rejected setups and no-trade days as well as executed trades.
Before entry
After exit
Date, time, account and strategy version
Entry/exit timestamps and actual average fills
Symbol, exchange, feed and timeframe
Actual filled quantity and all costs
Reason the setup qualifies
Net P/L and net R
Exact trigger, maximum entry and invalidation
Largest adverse/favourable movement if known
Stop, target, risk budget and size
Rule compliance: yes/no and the specific deviation
Relevant news / scheduled event check
Before/after screenshots and one improvement
A useful one-sentence review
Weak: "I lost because the market hates me." Better: "I entered before the 5-minute candle
closed; the signal did not meet rule 4." Also useful: "Every rule was met and the trade lost;
include it in the unchanged strategy sample."
Compare only comparable trades
Tag a manual TradingView paper trade separately from an ADRIAN/Alpaca paper trade. Your
course opening-range strategy differs from ADRIAN’s current research screen. Different
signals, feeds, account budgets or exit rules should not be mixed into one claim of strategy
performance.
END-OF-DAY HABIT
Write: one thing followed well, one mistake or uncertainty, and one specific task for
tomorrow. Then stop reviewing. Repeatedly reopening the chart to wish for a different
result does not improve the record.

pages.title: Measure expectancy, not just win rate
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
24  /  37
07 / PERFORMANCE
Measure expectancy, not just win rate
The central calculation
Net expectancy per trade = win rate × average net win - loss rate × average net loss. Use
positive magnitudes for average loss. Include losing trades, costs and unchanged rules. If
expectancy is negative, making more trades generally makes the problem bigger.
Hypothetical 20-trade sample
Amount
Winners
8 trades, average net win $8
Losers
12 trades, average net loss $5
Win rate
8 / 20 = 40%
Net expectancy
0.40 × $8 - 0.60 × $5 = $0.20 per trade
Total net P/L
8 × $8 - 12 × $5 = $4
Profit factor
$64 gross of winning net results / $60 losing net
results = 1.07
This is a tiny, fragile positive sample. If average loss rises from $5 to $5.50, expectancy
becomes -$0.10. A few dollars of extra friction can remove the apparent edge. Do not
extrapolate a small paper sample into a salary.
Break-even win rate
With average win W and average loss L, break-even win rate = L / (W + L), when those
averages already include costs. With $8 winners and $5 losers it is 5 / 13, approximately
38.46%. This is a description of those payoff assumptions, not a forecast of your win rate.
TRACK THESE TOO
Maximum drawdown, longest losing streak, costs, average result per trade,
rule-compliance percentage and the number of independent sessions. Profit
concentrated in one unusually lucky day deserves extra scrutiny.

pages.title: Do not confuse a good story with an edge
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
25  /  37
07 / TEST QUALITY
Do not confuse a good story with an
edge
Four ways a test fools you
• Looking ahead: you choose or adjust a signal using information that was unavailable at the
time.
• Cherry-picking: you keep the obvious trends and remove the messy sessions or losses.
• Overfitting: you tweak parameters until one historical sample looks impressive.
• Unrealistic fills: you assume every touch fills and every stop exits exactly at its trigger.
A practical testing sequence
First learn the mechanics in replay. Next fix one strategy version and keep a separate
development sample. Then test it on later unseen sessions. Finally forward-paper trade in
current markets, logging every rule and actual broker fill. A cost-sensitive result that fails this
sequence is not ready to promote.
Why 30-50 trades is a starting review, not proof
A small sample helps uncover execution mistakes and whether your rules are clear. It is not
strong statistical evidence of reliable future returns. Trades taken in the same trend can be
correlated. More independent sessions and market conditions matter as well as the raw trade
count.
YOUR CURRENT ADRIAN CONTEXT
The earlier MSFT historical experiments in this project were negative after modeled
costs. They evaluated a specific fixed strategy and do not prove that every possible
setup fails. They also do not establish a profitable edge for ADRIAN. Keep current
execution in paper mode and demand measured results rather than confident
wording.
Exercise: increase modeled costs, shift the test to an unseen date range and count every signal. Does the apparent
edge survive? If not, record that result instead of quietly hiding it.

pages.title: The mistakes that damage a small account
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
26  /  37
08 / MINDSET
The mistakes that damage a small
account
Mistake
Replacement habit
Revenge trading after a loss
Pause; a new position needs a new complete signal and
remaining budget.
Fear of missing out
Respect maximum entry; missed moves are not debts you
must recover.
Moving a stop farther away
Keep invalidation fixed; reduce or close under the written
plan.
Averaging down without a tested rule
Do not add to a losing position in this beginner course.
Increasing size after a lucky winner
Keep percentage risk stable for the test batch.
Changing strategy after every loss
Review the sample, not the emotional impact of one trade.
Trading every headline or influencer call
Verify the source and price response; use your own written
rules.
Treating paper gains as live readiness
Review fill realism, drawdown and discipline first.
A reset script
"The last trade is finished. It does not change the next setup’s quality. My remaining daily
budget is ____. My next action is either a complete qualified plan or no trade." Say this before
considering another entry.
STOP FOR THE DAY WHEN
The daily loss limit is hit, you cannot explain the next trade, you cannot verify your
position, or you are trying to win back a specific amount. A planned stop protects both
money and your ability to evaluate the strategy.

pages.title: Use AI as a checked assistant
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
27  /  37
09 / ADRIAN & TRADINGVIEW
Use AI as a checked assistant
Your intended workflow
ADRIAN compares a limited candidate set, gathers market/news evidence, applies
deterministic paper risk checks and can email a proposal. You approve that exact proposal
by replying YES before expiry. It rechecks the setup and uses Alpaca’s paper API for an
eligible order. A submitted order is not a confirmed fill.
Three systems, three records
TradingView is your charting and manual-practice environment. ADRIAN stores research,
approvals and reports. Alpaca stores its simulated account, orders and fills. Do not assume
the built-in TradingView paper account matches Alpaca or that a chart alert establishes a
broker fill.
Data and automation boundaries
ADRIAN’s connected US-stock data uses Alpaca IEX, while GNews supplies news.
TradingView’s current terms restrict non-display use of its market data, including automated
trading and algorithmic decision-making. Do not route its chart/alert data into an automated
execution system without appropriate permission or licensing. Use permitted broker/provider
data for that workflow. [S15]
ASK THE MANAGER
"Show my actual paper account, positions, order statuses and approval journal.
Separate submitted orders from fills. What data failed, what was skipped, and what
remains unverified?"
The course opening-range setup and ADRIAN’s research-screen rules are different. Do not
call the course strategy automated merely because ADRIAN can place paper orders. They
need separate versioned tests and journals. AI explanations can be wrong; order parameters
and actual fills need independent checking.

pages.title: Understand exactly what YES authorizes
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
28  /  37
09 / APPROVALS & EXITS
Understand exactly what YES authorizes
Read the whole proposal
• Confirm PAPER ONLY, the symbol, whole-share quantity and direction.
• Read the entry condition, maximum permitted price, stop, target and expiry.
• Check the proposed loss budget against your own practice limits.
• Reply YES as the first line in the original thread only if you approve that entry and its stated
protective exits. Reply NO to decline.
• A late, unverified or mismatched reply should not authorize a trade. A changed setup
should be skipped.
What happens after approval
The app checks market-open status, recent IEX data, cash, existing positions/orders and risk
again. If checks pass, it submits a paper limit-entry bracket with a unique order ID. A network
error may leave submission uncertain; check the broker record instead of resending blindly.
After entry fills, the approved bracket stop-loss and take-profit are managed by the broker.
Those specified exits do not require another YES. They still carry the execution limitations of
their order types. The current app does not give the model unrestricted authority to rewrite
stops, trade live or close arbitrary positions on a whim.
Current schedules and an important distinction
The app’s configured defaults are a weekday proposal check at 9:45 AM and a daily Manager
report at 5:00 PM Toronto time, while the server and PC are on. A report can be sent even
when no trade qualifies. SMTP acceptance alone does not prove inbox delivery.
SESSION-END CHECK
An Alpaca bracket does not by itself guarantee your position will close before the
session ends. DAY entry expiry is not the same as a time-based position exit. Check
the broker directly and resolve remaining exposure using its documented controls if
you require strict day-only holding.

pages.title: Your 30-day course schedule
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
29  /  37
10 / PRACTICE PLAN
Your 30-day course schedule
Treat these as 30 learning days, not a promise to be profitable in a month. Advance only
when the task is completed. If a stage exposes mistakes, repeat it. Paper losses are useful
information when recorded honestly.
Days
Focus
Deliverable
1-3
Foundations and account safety
Know your account mode, data source, trading hours, costs
and settlement questions.
4-6
TradingView and order mechanics
Saved layout plus ten correct paper order/cancel/exit drills.
7-10
Candles, levels and risk math
Ten annotated charts and five correct position-size
calculations.
11-15
Unseen replay practice
Journal ten setups or disciplined no-trade decisions without
future information.
16-23
Forward paper trading
Follow one fixed version; record every signal and actual fill.
Do not force a trade quota.
24-27
Review and stress-test
Compute net expectancy, costs, drawdown and
compliance; compare rule failures with valid losses.
28-30
Repeat weak areas and assess
Complete the quiz and readiness rubric. Continue paper
trading if evidence or discipline is insufficient.
A useful daily time commitment
Allow roughly 20-30 minutes for a lesson or review plus an execution-practice window you
can actually monitor. Reading alone cannot teach fill handling. Watching charts all day
without a written plan cannot establish an edge.
IF YOU HAVE ONLY EVENINGS
Use historical replay for mechanics and reserve live-session paper practice for days
you can attend. Do not pretend an evening replay fill is a forward-paper result. You
can complete the course more slowly; there is no graduation deadline.

pages.title: A gate before risking real money
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
30  /  37
10 / READINESS
A gate before risking real money
Readiness check
Required evidence
Mechanics
Correct order type, quantity, account, cancel state and exit coverage in repeated
drills.
Consistent rules
One written strategy version; changes logged and tested separately.
Forward sample
At least 30-50 documented paper trades across multiple sessions, or a longer
period if few signals qualify.
Risk discipline
No stop widening or unplanned size increases; daily limits respected.
Results
Net outcomes and drawdown evaluated with realistic costs. Positive results are
necessary for an edge claim but insufficient proof.
Operational safety
You know how to inspect broker records, deal with uncertain submissions and
resolve exposure.
Canadian readiness
Suitable live broker/account, permitted workflow, funding/settlement rules and
tax-record plan confirmed.
Financial readiness
Only money you can afford to lose; no need for trading income to meet bills.
These are teaching gates, not certification or personalised investment advice. If the strategy
is negative after costs, execution is inconsistent or you cannot explain the risk, the decision
is to remain in paper practice. There is no requirement to trade live after completing this
course.
If you eventually choose a live pilot
Use the smallest practical size and an explicit loss budget, confirm all real fees and data
permissions, and expect paper and live fills to differ. Do not increase size because a short
pilot wins. The Alpaca account used in this course remains paper-only for your current
Canadian situation. [S3, S4]

pages.title: Ten questions before graduation
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
31  /  37
ASSESSMENT
Ten questions before graduation
Answer without looking at the next page. A passing score is at least 8/10, with questions 2, 3,
6 and 9 mandatory because they concern execution and risk. A score is not permission to
trade live.
• 1. Your chart shows a last trade at $50.00. The ask is $50.05. Is $50.00 guaranteed as your
buy fill?
• 2. Account equity is $2,000 and risk is 0.25%. Entry is $50.40, stop is $49.90 and cost
reserve is $1. How many whole shares fit the $5 total allowance?
• 3. A stop-loss triggers at $49.90. Is an exit at exactly $49.90 guaranteed? Explain.
• 4. What is the difference between TradingView Paper Trading and Alpaca Paper Trading?
• 5. Why should you wait for a confirmation candle to finish?
• 6. The daily loss cap is $20, losses plus costs already total $17, and the next planned loss is
$5. Should you enter?
• 7. With 40% wins averaging $8 net and 60% losses averaging $5 net, what is net
expectancy per trade?
• 8. Is a $51.40 target valid if strong nearby resistance is $50.70 and entry is $50.40 with a
$49.90 stop?
• 9. Your app times out after submission. Should you immediately resend the same order?
• 10. In Bar Replay, can you assume that orders in the ordinary broker trading panel execute
against the historical chart?
SHORT PRACTICAL TEST
Explain one real paper order row: its symbol, quantity, status, average fill, protective
exit coverage and account mode. If it is unfilled, say unfilled. If you have no position,
demonstrate with an order drill rather than inventing a trade.

pages.title: Check the reasoning, not just the answer
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
32  /  37
ASSESSMENT / ANSWERS
Check the reasoning, not just the
answer
• 1. No. Last trade and current executable quote are different. A marketable buy may fill
against the ask or multiple asks.
• 2. Eight shares. Equity × risk = $5; subtract $1 cost reserve, then $4 / $0.50 = 8. Position
cost is $403.20.
• 3. No. A stop-market exit can fill worse during a rapid move, gap or thin liquidity. A
stop-limit may not fill at all.
• 4. They are separate simulated accounts with separate orders, positions and balances.
They do not automatically synchronise.
• 5. An unfinished bar can move back below the trigger and fail the signal by its close. Acting
earlier changes the tested strategy.
• 6. No. Only $3 remains in the daily allowance; a $5 planned loss does not fit.
• 7. $0.20: 0.40 × $8 - 0.60 × $5. The small apparent edge is sensitive to costs and sample
uncertainty.
• 8. Not under the course assumptions. Only $0.30 room to resistance gives 0.6 gross
reward/risk, not the proposed 2R opportunity.
• 9. No. Check broker orders and positions, including the unique client order ID where
available. The first submission may already exist.
• 10. No. Ordinary paper/broker orders can continue to use real-time data during replay. Use
dedicated Replay Trading for historical simulation. [S13]
Review any missed question
Return to the relevant lesson and repeat its exercise. Mandatory risk/execution questions
must be answered correctly before you advance. A knowledgeable explanation plus a clean
order drill is more useful than memorising a formula.
COURSE COMPLETION
Write your current decision: continue mechanics practice, continue forward paper
testing, revise and retest a strategy, or investigate a small live pilot with a suitable
Canadian broker. Include evidence and what remains uncertain.

LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE

Your one-page trade plan

FINAL GATE
Fresh data? Confirmation complete? Correct account? Risk and cash fit? Exit plan

pages.title: The plain-English trading glossary
pages.text:
ADRIAN.AI  /  DAY TRADING FOUNDATIONS
LEARN  •  PRACTISE  •  MEASURE
35  /  37
REFERENCE / KEEP HANDY
The plain-English trading glossary
Term
Meaning
Ask / bid
Displayed selling / buying interest; not guaranteed available size.
Spread
Difference between ask and bid.
Liquidity
How practically you can trade size without large price impact.
Slippage
Difference between expected and actual fill price.
OHLC
Open, high, low and close for a candle period.
Support / resistance
Areas where buying / selling previously interrupted movement.
Opening range
High and low of your defined first-session time window.
VWAP
Volume-weighted average price for a chosen anchor period.
Invalidation
The observable condition that says the planned setup no longer holds.
R
One unit of planned price risk; net results also include costs.
Bracket / linked exits
Entry plus protective stop/target instructions with broker-specific linking.
Partial fill
Only part of the requested quantity executed.
Drawdown
Decline from a prior equity peak.
Expectancy
Average result expected under observed win/loss/payoff assumptions.
Profit factor
Total positive results divided by absolute total negative results.
Forward paper / replay
Current-market simulation / historical practice with future bars hidden.
IEX / consolidated feed
One venue’s data / combined data from multiple markets.
T+1
Settlement generally one business day after the trade; instrument rules differ.
